title: This Teen's Plant-Based Plastic Could Help Clean Up Microplastics
summary: Microplastics are everywhere — in oceans, soil, food, and even the air we breathe. Because they're so tiny, removing them is incredibly difficult. But 18-year-old Arya Satheesh from Ireland has developed a clever solution: Eco Purge, a plant-based plastic that naturally decomposes while helping break down microplastics already in the environment. Arya first became interested in microplastics in 2024, when she created a water-quality sensor for a national science competition. Her device could detect microplastics in water, but it couldn't remove them. Determined to fix that, she began developing Eco Purge. To make the bioplastic, she needed two natural enzymes. She contacted several biotechnology companies for samples. Some offered to sell them to her, but they were too expensive for a high school student. Undeterred, Arya reached out to Professor Kevin O'Connor, a researcher at BiOrbic in Ireland. Sure enough, O'Connor was able to obtain the enzyme samples. He also helped her gain access to a laboratory at a local university, where she could develop Eco Purge. By early 2026, Arya had her first prototype. She tested it by placing a set amount of microplastic with Eco Purge in soil, salt water, and fresh water. She observed the samples for six weeks. To her delight, at the end of the trial, both the microplastic and Eco Purge had decomposed in each sample. Her invention earned her the European regional title at The Earth Prize in May 2026, along with $12,500 in prize money and access to experts to help her develop the project further. Arya still faces challenges before Eco Purge can be widely available: the enzymes only work on certain types of plastic, high temperatures can damage them, and producing large amounts of enzymes could be expensive. But she's determined to overcome these hurdles and keep improving Eco Purge. "Science isn't just about understanding the world," she reflects. "It's about leaving it better than we found it."
why_it_matters: Microplastics have turned up in rivers, farmland and even human blood, so a cheap biological way to break them down could change how cities and factories deal with plastic waste. The story also shows that teenagers with a good mentor and lab access can push real research forward, not just big companies.

background_read: Arya Satheesh (an 18-year-old student inventor from Ireland) built Eco Purge with help from BiOrbic, an Irish research centre that studies how plants, microbes and waste can replace oil-based materials, and from Professor Kevin O'Connor, the researcher there who got her the enzymes and lab space.
The Earth Prize, the contest Arya won in May 2026, is a global competition for teenage environmental inventors that rewards winners with money and expert mentors.
Microplastics, the pollution Eco Purge targets, are plastic fragments so small — often like grains of sand or smaller — that water filters and clean-up boats simply cannot catch them.
Enzymes are proteins made by living things that speed up chemical reactions: the ones in your stomach digest food, and certain microbial enzymes can break plastic apart.

Scientists in Japan found a bacterium living at a plastic-recycling plant that produces an enzyme able to break down PET, the plastic used in drink bottles — which is why researchers now take plastic-eating enzymes seriously as a clean-up tool.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — young inventors and science competitions
perspectives.description: Arya turned a school science project into a working prototype and an international prize. Her route — asking companies, then a university professor, for help — shows that persistence and mentors can open doors that money alone cannot.

Enzymes are fragile, attack only some plastics, and could be expensive to make in bulk. Critics warn that exciting 'clean-up' technology can distract governments and companies from the harder job of producing less plastic in the first place.

Eco Purge fits a wider pattern called bioremediation, where living things are used to undo human pollution. Nature adapting to eat our waste is promising, but a six-week lab trial and an industrial factory are very different tests.

The next steps are cheaper enzyme production and trials in real wastewater plants or compost sites. If those work, future plastics could be designed with their own disposal built in, so waste breaks down where it lands.
